title: Visa V Stock and Mastercard MA Test Record Highs as Trump Accounts Buying Fuels Momentum - FXLeaders
content: Visa and Mastercard shares surged more than 3% on Monday, strengthening their market leadership as strong earnings, institutional buying and renewed investor confidence pushed both payment giants toward major technical resistance levels. Visa (V) shares extended their advance, moving toward the $300 level after breaking to fresh highs and attracting renewed interest from institutional investors. The latest rally reflects a combination of strong financial performance, improving analyst sentiment and expectations that Visa can continue benefiting from resilient consumer spending and rising digital payments. Visa’s fiscal third-quarter 2026 results provided a strong fundamental backdrop. Revenue increased 14% year over year to $11.6 billion, while earnings per share reached $3.32, beating analyst expectations. The company also raised its full-year outlook, reinforcing confidence in its growth trajectory. Investor sentiment received another boost after Pershing Square’s Bill Ackman disclosed an approximately $1.1 billion stake in Visa. The high-profile investment added further credibility to the bullish case, while analysts at Truist, Cantor Fitzgerald and Wells Fargo recently raised their price targets. With shares pushing higher, the $300 level is becoming an increasingly important psychological and technical target. A sustained move above it could strengthen the bullish trend, although the sharp rally also leaves the stock vulnerable to profit-taking. Mastercard (MA) also surged more than 3%, bringing the stock back toward the $600 area and its previous record high. The move has placed Mastercard at a critical technical level, with investors watching whether the shares can decisively break above the prior peak. Mastercard recently reported quarterly earnings per share of $5.04 and revenue of $9.28 billion, with both figures exceeding analyst expectations. The results highlighted continued operational strength and resilient demand for the company’s global payment network. Mastercard also paid a quarterly dividend of $0.87 per share on August 7, providing an additional source of shareholder returns and supporting the stock’s appeal to institutional investors. Recent financial disclosure filings also revealed that investment accounts associated with President Trump purchased millions of dollars worth of Visa and Mastercard shares during June. The purchases were part of a broader series of transactions that included Berkshire Hathaway and Cintas, while the largest individual transaction disclosed was a sale of between $5 million and $25 million of the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF. The disclosure has added another layer of attention around the payment stocks as both companies approach historically significant levels. The latest rally has created a powerful momentum trade across the payments sector. Strong earnings, institutional buying, positive analyst revisions and continued shareholder returns have all reinforced the bullish narrative. However, Visa’s approach toward $300 and Mastercard’s test of $600 could prove decisive. A clean breakout above these resistance zones could open the door to further gains, while another failure near record highs could trigger profit-taking after the recent surge. For now, Visa and Mastercard remain among the strongest performers in the payments sector, but their ability to hold these elevated levels will determine whether the latest rally develops into a sustained breakout or another rejection at record highs.

title: DOWN To Release "Volume V" Full-Length November 20th - Premier Guitar
content: American heavy metal icons DOWN will unleash their long-awaited new studio album, Volume V, on November 20th via Nuclear Blast Records! American heavy metal icons DOWN will unleash their long-awaited new studio album, Volume V, on November 20th via Nuclear Blast Records! DOWN was never just a band. It’s a brotherhood rooted in childhood friendships that have endured for decades. It’s an homage to the city of New Orleans, Louisiana. It’s music meant for anybody who has ever headbanged, played air guitar, or worn a weathered tour t-shirt like armor. For over three decades, the quintet – Philip H. Anselmo, Pepper Keenan, Kirk Windstein, Jimmy Bower, and Pat Bruders – have quietly built a legacy like no other. When these individuals congregate, magic ensues, conjured by earthquaking grooves, bellowing straight from the soul, and riffing loud enough to awaken an ancient deity. This Fall, DOWN begins another chapter with Volume V. “We were all excited about this,” smiles Anselmo. “There was a sense of lightness in the air. Everyone’s attitude was positive. There was more focus than ever. It just felt fresh again. Each one of us was individually striving for something, and I believe we achieved what we wanted to achieve. The record is a journey. It’s classic DOWN, but it’s also unique.” “Everybody played their asses off, wrote great riffs, and Philip is singing amazing,” adds Windstein. “There’s so much electricity when we get together. To me, it’s the same vibe as our debut NOLA, but we’ve got another 35 years of experience as songwriters.” “The five of us are from the same era, grew up together, and accomplished a lot on our own,” Keenan observes. “We all sounded different, but we’re still from the same 20-block radius. As far as what makes DOWN special, we knew one another before any of us had done anything. There’s history.” DOWN’s bond runs deep. The guys initially crossed paths as teens in various local bands throughout New Orleans. Over the years, each musician went off and made a name for himself with Anselmo notably fronting Pantera, Keenan holding down guitar and vocals for Corrosion Of Conformity, Windstein leading Crowbar, and Bower slinging guitar in Eyehategod. Two writing sessions yielded the bulk of material on Volume V. Upholding a tradition dating back to Down II, the members retreated to Anselmo’s home studio and their de facto clubhouse, Nodferatu’s Lair. Songs originated on the spot as they jammed face-to-face. Throughout 2025, the music naturally took shape. Keenan and Windstein chose to simultaneously record guitar together, giving the album a timeless punch. The album opens with a blistering barnburner “The Myth.” It sets the tone with a powerhouse vocal, pummeling rhythms, and precise down-picking. Then, there’s “Merciful Fate” featuring King Diamond. It reaches an apex with a vocal duel between Anselmo and King Diamond and fret-burning solos executed at a breakneck pace of 120bpm. King’s wife Livia Zita even blesses the track with dark accents of her own. Closer “Twice-Told Tales” caps the trip off with a heavy and hypnotic denouement. “It’s a conglomerate of tight riffs and blues rock mixed with the diligence of classic metal,” Anselmo reveals. “It’s an important song to us. I could feel Ozzy Osbourne’s influence on me in the strangest way.” Lead single, “Blood Oath,” is anchored by an alternately hard-hitting and hummable riff, culminating on a clarion call chorus. With a sly tip of the hat to their stomping grounds, it practically bleeds old gold, black, and white. “Anybody who’s from New Orleans is going to get a kick out of the references to the city,” grins Anselmo. “Musically, it’s got a big hook. It’s a DOWN song, but it takes a turn.” “You’ll know it’s DOWN right off the fucking bat,” adds Keenan. “It’s heavy in its attack.” DOWN’s Volume V was produced by Eddie Mapp and DOWN, mixed by Dave Fortman, and mastered by Maor Appelbaum at Maor Appelbaum Mastering  in California. In October, DOWN will perform at both Aftershock and Sick New World Texas. In December the band will headline day two (December 5th) of this year’s edition of the Decibel Magazine Metal & Beer Fest Denver. title: Fulham 2-3 Chelsea: Rogers and Palmer star as Sanchez struggles - how the players rated - BBC
content: Morgan Rogers scored 41 minutes into his Premier League debut for Chelsea Morgan Rogers scored on his Chelsea debut as Xabi Alonso's side beat Fulham at Craven Cottage. The £117m signing slotted in his side's second goal after Fulham midfielder Josh King had cancelled out Joao Pedro's opener, which came within 31 seconds. Cole Palmer thought he had sealed victory for Chelsea with a third goal early in the second half before debutant striker Gonzalo Garcia gave Fulham hope but the visitors held on to start the season with a win. Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them at the bottom of the page too. Palmer shines as Chelsea edge Fulham in Alonso debut win Three reasons Chelsea could challenge for title - and one they may not Palmer shines as Alonso begins Chelsea reign with win at Fulham Bernd Leno: The German goalkeeper was not particularly at fault for any of Chelsea's goals but still couldn't stop them. 5 Timothy Castagne: The right-back set up King's goal and his shot led to Fulham's second, but he struggled defensively. 6 Jorge Cuenca: His poor clearance and mistimed tackle led to Chelsea's opening goal. He was also at fault for the second, failing to stop Lacroix's cross. However, his lofted pass helped create Fulham's second goal. 4 Calvin Bassey: Less culpable than many of his defensive team-mates, but still part of a disappointing display at the back. 5 Antonee Robinson: The United States international produced an important early block from a Rogers effort and delivered an excellent cross later in the first half, but was often caught out of position on the counter-attack. He lofted a finish well wide in the 77th minute with his weaker right foot when one-on-one with Sanchez. 6 Sander Berge: Struggled to dictate the tempo as he had done in pre-season in an unsettled game. 5 Josh King: The academy graduate was Fulham's standout performer, creating chances and posing a threat before scoring the first-half equaliser. Almost produced an equaliser in the 73rd minute from range. 8 Alex Iwobi: The Nigeria international provided a strong physical presence both defensively and in attack. 6 Oscar Bobb: The Norway international's direct running caused problems down the right, although his influence faded as the game wore on. 7 Gonzalo Garcia: On his debut, Garcia provided a useful focal point in attack in a difficult match for Fulham. He helped relieve pressure after long spells of Chelsea possession and was rewarded with a close-range header in the second half. 7 Cesar Palacios: The new signing worked hard on his debut, but little came off for him, including a long-range effort that flew well over the bar in the first half. 5 Shea Charles (on 67, Bobb): The new signing from Southampton produced some dangerous long balls as Fulham pushed for an equaliser. 6 Kevin (on 73, Palacios): Did little to influence the game. 5 Ryan Sessegnon (on 73, Berge): His running in-behind threatened down the left and he forced a good save from Sanchez. 6 Subs not used: Lecomte, De Gougerolles, Tete, Reed, Kevin, Smith Rowe. Robert Sanchez: An early kicking error gifted Fulham a corner. He should have saved King's equaliser at his near post, while his initial save for Fulham's second was parried into a dangerous area, allowing Garcia to score. 3 Josh Acheampong: The 20-year-old produced a fine double clearance and block in the 27th minute and looked solid throughout. 6 Maxence Lacroix: Remarkably involved in both of Chelsea's first two goals, with his headed clearance leading to the opener and his run down the right and cut-back setting up Rogers. 7 Levi Colwill: An early mistake left him fortunate to escape with only a yellow card after a foul on Bobb. He was also partly at fault for Fulham's second goal after failing to clear a deep cross. 5 Malo Gusto: The wing-back was a surprise selection amid Chelsea's injury problems, but his passing lacked conviction at times. 5 Romeo Lavia: Booked early on after a late challenge on Bassey. He grew into the game, however, going close from a corner and moving the ball well through midfield. 5 Reece James: Saw a miscued effort saved in the first half but gradually grew into the game and helped Chelsea gain control. 6 Jorrel Hato: Operating in an unfamiliar wing-back role, the defender produced a promising early dribble and adapted well. 6 Cole Palmer: Simply the best player on the pitch. Palmer was creative, physically impressive and produced several superb dribbles before scoring an excellent third goal. He looks refreshed after the summer break. 9 Morgan Rogers: An outstanding debut. Pressed aggressively, had a shot blocked, played in Joao Pedro and then capped his display by scoring Chelsea's second with a far-post finish. 8 Joao Pedro: Opened the scoring after 31 seconds with a deft finish over Leno. He also exploited Fulham's high defensive line intelligently to set up Palmer's goal. 8 Enzo Fernandez (on 65, Lavia): The Argentine was booed by the home fans on every touch of the ball and might not have featured had Moises Caicedo been fit. Still, Fernandez moved the ball around the pitch and fought for possession. 6 Pep Chavarria (on 65, Hato): It was a back-to-the-wall job for the wing-back but he did little of note on his brief debut cameo. 5 'To have a good team, we need a great Cole' - Alonso After the opportunity to rate players has closed, the score displayed represents the average from all the submissions by BBC Sport users. title: The Hybrid SUV That’s Perfect For First-Time Buyers - Top Speed
content: Hybrid vehicles have never been more relevant — or more competitive. Walk into any segment of the SUV market right now and you'll find a hybrid option waiting for you.     mainstream automakers have hybrid SUVs in their portfolio; be it compact, midsize, or full-size. If you're shopping for a hybrid SUV for the first time, the sheer number of choices can be overwhelming, because nearly every model brings something genuinely compelling to the table. What most first-time buyers actually want, though, is simpler than the spec sheets suggest: a capable engine, real-world fuel savings, a comfortable and well-equipped cabin, inoffensive styling, and a price that doesn't require a deep breath before signing. One SUV consistently checks every one of those boxes — and its sales figures prove it isn't a secret. That SUV is this Japanese crossover from Honda. There's a reason it ranks among the best-selling hybrid vehicles in the U.S. — and if you're a first-time hybrid buyer, it deserves a very close look. The Honda CR-V Hybrid has held a commanding position in its segment for several years running. Although Honda introduced America's first mainstream hybrid car, the Insight, Toyota has long been synonymous with hybrid technology. The fact that Toyota fields nearly 20 hybrids in its lineup while Honda offers just three hasn't changed that perception. Even so, the CR-V Hybrid managing to outsell its archnemesis in arguably the most popular and crowded hybrid segment in the industry is a powerful statement about what Honda has built. Its neutral yet far-from-boring styling, combined with an impressive feature set inside and out, makes the CR-V Hybrid a default choice for buyers shopping the hybrid market under $50,000. That said, look closely and you'll find a few areas where it doesn't lead the pack. Its engine is smaller and produces less power than the Toyota RAV4 Hybrid or the Kia Sportage Hybrid. It's also pricier than both rivals at the base trim level, and it's offered in just three trims compared to the RAV4 Hybrid's seven. But taken as a whole, the package is compelling enough that the CR-V Hybrid is very hard to argue against. The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid is offered in three trims, ranging from $35,630 to $42,550. While the trim lineup is narrower than some rivals, Honda keeps things focused and ensures each level offers genuine value. Every CR-V Hybrid trim shares the same powertrain: a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine paired with two electric motors fed by a 1.1 kWh battery pack. The combined output is 204 horsepower — 14 more than the standard CR-V produces. Front-wheel drive is standard on the Sport Hybrid and Sport-L Hybrid trims, with AWD available as an option. An eCVT handles power delivery to the wheels. On the top-spec Sport Touring Hybrid, all-wheel drive is included as standard equipment. 2.0-liter Four-Cylinder And Two Permanent-Magnet Motors 2.0-liter Four-Cylinder And Two Permanent-Magnet Motors In terms of fuel efficiency, the Honda CR-V Hybrid returns up to 40 MPG combined in the FWD model and 37 MPG combined in the AWD trim. That translates to an overall range of approximately 560 miles and 518 miles, respectively. Compared to the fuel costs of an average new vehicle, you'll save up to $2,500 with the FWD model and $2,000 with the AWD model over five years. These are EPA-estimated savings based on 45-percent highway, 55-percent city driving, and 15,000 miles per year, and reflect prevailing fuel prices at the time of calculation. The CR-V Hybrid comes with heated front seats, a moonroof, a six-speaker audio system, dual-zone climate control, and more in the base trim. The seven-inch touchscreen supports both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. Step up the trim ladder, and you gain a nine-inch touchscreen with wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay compatibility. The six-speaker audio system gives way to an eight-speaker Bose setup, and additional conveniences include a wireless charger, a satellite-linked navigation system, and Smart Entry with Walk Away Auto Lock. Honda equips every CR-V Hybrid with its Honda Sensing suite of driver-assistive technologies, on top of additional features like the Blind Spot Information System and Cross Traffic Monitor. The Honda Sensing Driver Assistive Features include: Honda's warranty isn't quite at the level of Kia or Hyundai, but it aligns with industry norms. Coverage includes a three-year or 36,000-mile limited warranty and a five-year or 60,000-mile powertrain warranty. Replaced parts carry a one-year warranty, and you can also opt for the 36-month or 36,000-mile roadside assistance coverage. The Honda CR-V Hybrid is a genuinely reliable vehicle. J.D. title: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy - Constitutional Accountability Center
content: In St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, the Supreme Court is considering whether the Free Exercise Clause requires Colorado to allow religious preschool providers to join its state-funded universal preschool program even though they refuse to comply with the state’s neutral and generally applicable rule barring discrimination against children and families based on sexual orientation and gender identity. Colorado administers a universal preschool program (UPK) that offers free preschool for four-year-olds statewide. Private preschools that participate in the voluntary program—whether secular or religious—receive taxpayer funds to cover the costs of educating these students. To participate, eligible preschools must abide by the state program’s nondiscrimination policy, which requires that preschools not discriminate against either children or parents based on, among other traits, sexual orientation or gender identity. This requirement applies to all preschools participating in Colorado’s UPK program, and there is no pathway for any preschool to be exempted from the program’s ban on discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Two Catholic parishes that run (or ran) a preschool filed suit, along with the Archdiocese of Denver and two parents with preschool-age children. They argued that Colorado’s refusal to exempt them from the UPK program’s nondiscrimination policy violates the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause by excluding preschools and families from receiving state benefits because of their religion. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit upheld the Colorado program.  The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case, and CAC filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of First Amendment scholars in support of Colorado. Our brief makes two principal points. First, it argues that Founding-era history regarding the free exercise of religion does not support the petitioners’ claim that they are entitled to an exemption from a neutral and generally applicable civil law. Several Founding-era state constitutions included provisions that protected the free exercise of religion but also made clear that individuals were not permitted to violate the peace and safety of other citizens in the exercise of their religion. Further, Founding-era congressional debates support the view that the Free Exercise Clause was not understood to have conferred a broad religious exemption from compliance with civil laws. Second, the brief explains why ruling for petitioners would require the Court to depart from decades of precedent, including Employment Division v. Smith and cases both before and after it. Pre-Smith precedent made clear that the government has both a compelling interest in eradicating discrimination and broad authority to conduct its internal affairs without conforming to every individual’s religious views. Smith itself held that where “prohibiting or burdening the free exercise of religion ‘is not the object [of a law] but merely the incidental effect of a generally applicable and otherwise valid provision, the First Amendment has not been offended.’” And no case since Smith has suggested that neutral and generally applicable policies like Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement must yield to requests for religious exemptions. Under the Court’s precedents, when “followers of a particular sect enter into commercial activity as a matter of choice”—like running a preschool that seeks to join Colorado’s UPK program—“the limits they accept on their own conduct as a matter of conscience and faith are not to be superimposed on the statutory schemes which are binding on others in that activity.” Taken together, this body of precedent leads to the conclusion that the petitioners have no right to participate in voluntary state-funded programs without complying with the government’s nondiscrimination policy for all participants.

title: Amicus Brief: Tedford’s Tenancy v. City of New York and Walls v. Prince George’s County - Manhattan Institute
content: Don't miss the newsletters from MI and City Journal Tedford’s Tenancy owns a rent-stabilized apartment building in New York City, and its necessary expenses will always exceed the rental income permitted by the government’s rent ceilings. Garnell Walls wants to build a home on his property in Prince George’s County, Maryland, but the county will not approve the private well and septic system he needs to do so. Both property owners sued, arguing that the restrictions on their properties were unconstitutional takings of their property without just compensation. But neither plaintiff’s claim was allowed to proceed in court. The New York courts held that Tedford's Tenancy first had to pursue preexisting hardship exemptions, even though Tedford is ineligible for them and, in any event, wouldn't really help their financial dire straits. The Fourth Circuit held that Walls had gone to court too soon because he had not sought a “legislative amendment” from the county, which also wouldn't help Walls's situation. Now on petition for Supreme Court review, the Manhattan Institute and Professor James W. Ely, Jr. have filed an amicus brief supporting both property owners’ petitions for Supreme Court review. These cases implicate the “finality requirement” for regulatory-takings claims. Under Supreme Court precedent, a property owner may bring a takings claim once the government has reached a conclusive position about how its regulations apply to the property. The owner need not first exhaust every remaining governmental procedure. Yet some lower courts continue to treat finality as a matter of “prudential ripeness,” allowing them to impose judge-made barriers to takings claims. The Court should clarify that finality is a jurisdictional requirement grounded in Article III standing, not a prudential doctrine that courts may use to impose additional barriers to takings claims. The Court should grant the petitions and put an end to the second-class treatment of property rights under the prudential-ripeness doctrine. As hard as it may be to believe now, there was a time, in the not-so-distant past, when every Lamborghini to leave Sant'Agata Bolognese was a stick shift. But then in 2004, three years into the Murciélago's reign atop the brand's lineup, the company unveiled a new six-speed "e-Gear" automated manual gearbox. The e-Gear, which utilized paddle shifters, allowed for rapid gear changes without the use of a clutch pedal and would soon supplant the manual as the marque's transmission of choice. In fact, by 2013, less than a decade after the e-Gear's debut, Lamborghini released its last car to feature a manual, the Gallardo LP 560-2 50th Anniversario. The Murciélago LP 670-4 SV may not be the last Raging Bull stick shift, but it is the last of the company's flagship V-12's to include the gearbox. Unveiled in 2009, the year before the model was replaced by the Aventador, the SV is a high-performance, track-focused variant that was designed and engineered to be the most hardcore version of the outgoing supercar. It has a more aggressive aero package, a modified suspension, and the most potent version of the model's naturally aspirated 12-cylinder, which could produce 670 hp and 487 ft lbs of torque. Lamborghini announced plans to build 350 examples of the vehicle, but only 268 are thought to have actually left the factory. Of those, only five rolled off the line equipped with a six-speed manual. The example up for auction was the last to leave the factory and thus is believed to be Lamborghini's final V-12 manual, according to the auction house. That alone makes the car noteworthy, but it is also the only example finished in a dazzling coat of Ad Personam Marrone Eklipsis over a two-tone Marrone Janus and Avorio Lilium leather interior. The car, which is also one of just three equipped with a low-drag wing, had just 4,912 miles on it at the time of cataloging, suggesting that it remains in impeccable shape. RM Sotheby's is offering this Murciélago LP 670-4 SV without reserve. That means there's no public sale estimate, but the auction house sold another Super Veloce, this one with an e-Gear transmission, for $3.14 million earlier this month. title: New merger, one canceled season as Section V football scrimmages near - Democrat and Chronicle
content: There is less than a week until kickoff of the Section V high school football season with scrimmages scheduled for this weekend. This is the first season in years in which all teams are under one umbrella. There are no breakaway groups or leagues, like the Wayne-Finger Lakes Independent. Every team is eligible to play in sectionals, the area's high school football playoffs. Not enough players came out for the team at Mynderse Academy this preseason. An arrangement was made for 12 Mynderse players to join the Waterloo Tigers, coached by Tyrone Thomas, this fall. "It's relatively new," Mynderse athletic director Kevin Korzeniewski said, adding that Waterloo is "hosting" the merger and had enough players to continue in 2026. "Mynderse has low numbers this year." The new Waterloo/Mynderse team will compete in Class B this season. Three home games take place at Waterloo and one at Mynderse Academy. "We're talking about that now," Korzeniewski said. "We were a D, Waterloo a C." Low participation numbers ended the season of the Wilson/Early College Wildcats before Week 1 in Section V. "We're all battling that," Section V football coordinator Tyler Winter said. Wilson athletic director Eric Mundorff said the Wildcats hope to play at the junior varsity level instead. The two withdrawals from the season leave holes in the Wayne-Finger Lakes League and Rochester City Athletic Conference schedules. Edison/Padilla at Franklin/School of the Arts/School Without Walls, another team in the RCAC, is back in Class AA after being listed in Class A2. title: Upgradeable PC doubles as a Steam gaming console for your living room - New Atlas
content: Valve's Steam Machine is the gaming system that PC gamers have been dreaming of for years. Sadly, it's hard to get your hands on one, and it costs a pretty penny. This new mini PC with some clever tricks up its sleeve might be just the thing to shop for instead. Like the Steam Machine, the Piston V packs powerful hardware into a compact form factor, and then takes things a whole lot further. It's got a circular 4-inch touchscreen that makes it easy to boot into Windows for work, or SteamOS-like Bazzite to play games. That means you don't need to splurge on a separate console to get your gaming fix. The PC is under 6 inches (14.6 cm) tall, so you can quickly move it from your workspace to your living room and plug into your TV for big-screen playtime. Piston V | Dual-OS Gaming Beast in a Gadget Form Factor While the Piston V will run Linux-based Bazzite out of the box, you can replace it with a SteamOS installation without spending a dime. That unlocks the best bits of the Steam Machine experience: the ability to pause your game anytime and instantly resume from where you left off, access to some 18,000 compatible titles, and smooth performance thanks to the lack of bloatware. Plus, the Piston V is upgradeable, so you can increase its onboard storage and RAM whenever you like, via easily accessible storage slots on the back of the device. So what does this baby have under the hood? You're looking at an AMD AI 365 Zen 5 CPU, an 880M RDNA 3.5 GPU, 16GB DDR5 RAM, and a 500GB SSD. That's a better processor than you'll get in the Steam Machine. The Piston V will support upgrades to 64GB RAM and up to 4TB of storage. For connectivity, you've got a nice selection of ports that are ideal for gaming: That's a pretty good configuration which can run a variety of games at high refresh rates, including graphics-intensive titles like Cyberpunk 2077. Game consoles have become less compelling and more expensive lately (yup, Xbox AND PlayStation), so this seems like a terrific option if you're open to PC gaming or already have a library of games. The Piston V is being crowdfunded on Kickstarter, where it can be had for as little as US$559 at the time of writing. It goes up incrementally as units get spoken for – but even so, you're essentially getting a $1,049 Steam Machine's worth of hardware and then some for roughly half the price. All crowdfunding campaigns carry an element of risk, so you'll want to keep that in mind if you choose to back this campaign. It's also worth noting this is the first product from the team behind the Piston V. That said, it's shown off working PCs on its campaign page, and has had a review unit put through its paces by notable gaming YouTube ETA PRIME. The Piston V has also racked up more than $175,000 from 300 backers at this point. The team notes that with today's volatile RAM and storage prices, it will end up making a loss on early bird orders, as part of its effort to gain traction. I appreciate the transparency there, particularly in this climate where hardware components are frightfully pricey. If all goes to plan, orders are slated to ship worldwide starting December 2026. You'll be able to select RAM and SSD upgrades before the campaign ends. Note: New Atlas may earn commission from purchases made via links.

title: Champion Welcomes V of BTS as the Face of Its New ‘True Champion’ Campaign - New Wave Magazine
content: Champion is entering a new chapter with ‘True Champion’, a global campaign celebrating the athletes, artists and creatives redefining what it means to be a champion. Leading the campaign is V of BTS, whose influence across music, fashion and popular culture makes him a natural fit for the brand. The campaign moves beyond traditional ideas of athleticism, instead focusing on individuality, creativity and the impact people can have simply by being themselves. Alongside V, the FW26 campaign features a diverse cast spanning sport, music and culture, including Romeo Beckham, SOFI TUKKER, Kyle Kuzma and Danna Paola. V's presence feels particularly fitting given his established relationship with fashion. Known for his distinctive personal style, he has become increasingly influential beyond music, bringing the same sense of individuality to his approach to clothing and visual culture. From a styling perspective, what stands out is how naturally Champion's aesthetic works with V's understated approach. The campaign imagery keeps the clothing grounded and wearable, allowing the classic Champion identity to sit alongside a more contemporary, fashion-conscious sensibility. Rather than positioning the campaign around one definition of success, ‘True Champion’ feels more interested in what makes someone memorable. It is a message that extends beyond sport and into the wider creative industries, where originality and authenticity increasingly carry as much weight as performance With the campaign launching globally from 10 August 2026, Champion is using its century-long sporting heritage to speak to a new generation of creatives. For a brand built around self-expression, V is a fitting face for what comes next. © 2023 by New Wave Magazine. Proudly created by New Wave Studios

Fans are asking Ram V for an Absolute Aquaman title, but he's got no plans to join the line Ram V may be one of DC's most popular writers of the last several years, but as of right now, he's got no plans to join the publisher's ultra-successful Absolute line, which reinvents classic characters with new origins and adventures, though he has been in touch with the line's de facto leader, Absolute Batman writer Scott Snyder. "I'm not doing anything on the Absolute side of things," V states in a League of Comic Geeks AMA when asked if he's considered an Absolute Aquaman title. "While Scott's been welcoming, I usually don't have books suggested to me. I've almost always picked the projects I'd like to work on. And I'd been doing so much superheroing, I felt the need to step away. My attention is largely focused on Deicidium for now. I'm glad everyone's enjoying staggering work on the Absolute stuff though!" Ram V recently finished up a two-year 'exclusive contract with DC. V did in fact write Aquaman once already in his cosmically esoteric Aquaman: Andromeda, created alongside artist Christian Ward, which pits the king of the seas against his old nemesis Black Manta, with a strange mystery brewing beneath the seas. But he's still unsure whether he'd go back to Arthur Curry whether in the main universe or the Absolute line. "Will I return to any character? Honestly depends on whether I have a meaningful story to tell or if I'm being offered something particularly interesting," V states, also clarifying that he doesn't necessarily have a list of characters he's looking to take on. "I don't really spend too much time thinking about what characters I'd like to write. I know I'd love to take on a Dr. Strange book at some point." title: The Used Luxury SUV That Makes A New CR-V Look Expensive - Top Speed
content: The Honda CR-V is one of the safer bets in the compact-SUV market, but demand has caused its prices to climb the MSRP ladder to the point that newer-model-year used options have become viable considerations. The range-topping 2026 Sport Touring Hybrid, for example, clocks in at $42,550, with standard all-wheel drive, leather seating, premium audio, and a 204-horsepower dual-motor hybrid powertrain. In all fairness, that is a lot of sensible SUV for the money, but it costs enough to warrant a look at compact luxury SUV models that have recently come on the used-car market. A buyer willing to look at two-, three-, four- or five-year-old vehicles will find luxury-brand SUVs for about the same price, having depreciation do the bulk of the price-equality work. Depreciation is the great equalizer in the used-car market, and it is relentless when it comes to luxury vehicles. Buyers who wouldn’t chance a glance at a $60,000-plus luxury SUV even a couple years ago can consider it instead of the mainstream SUV that fits comfortably into their monthly budget. Luxury SUVs depreciate more quickly because of their high purchase prices and rapid technology upgrades. The average vehicle loses about 40 to 50 percent of its value over its first five years, with luxury vehicles at the top end of that range. For comparison, SUVs are about in the middle of that range, and luxury SUV depreciation ranges from 45 to 55 percent, and about 30 to 35 percent over its first two years. Working backwards with that math, a $42,550 2026 Honda CR-V (the top-of-the-line Sport Touring Hybrid) carries a price equivalent to a 2023 $65,000 luxury SUV. At $42,550, the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid sits justifiably at the top of the CR-V lineup, with a standard equipment list that includes a 204-horsepower two-motor hybrid system, standard AWD, a five-mode drive selector, 19-inch gloss-black alloy wheels, leather-trimmed seats (heated in front), heated steering wheel, power sunroof, and dual-zone climate control. That price and level of standard equipment brings the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid to the borderline of luxury-SUV territory, combining the CR-V's everyday practicality with a distinctly upscale feature set. There is no mistaking it as a premium compact SUV (and a really good one, at that), though the mindset still remains with some buyers that it is just a gussied-up econobox SUV on which you compromise because you can’t afford the luxury compact SUV you really desire. Age needs context. A 2022 luxury SUV is not necessarily an old SUV in 2026. Some five-year-old models may still be on the current generation cycle, meaning the looks and mechanicals are still the same, and even some of the technology (though that sometimes changes dramatically from year to year). Barring mid-cycle refreshes, basic design, cabin architecture, safety features, and powertrain usually carry over. Even with mid-cycle refreshes, some luxury-SUV things don’t change. Buyers may have to accept that the technology has been upgraded over five years (sometimes overhauled), but carefully selected 2022–2025 SUVs still have contemporary driver-assistance systems, modern digital displays, premium audio systems, and contemporary comfort and convenience features. Take this standout that combines a prestigious badge, top-notch amenities and a high-performance powertrain. The 2022 BMW X3 M40i illustrates the benefits of depreciation particularly well, in terms of dollar value. Its original MSRP was $57,800 and Kelley Blue Book’s current Fair Purchase Price is listed at $39,400, translating into a depreciation of 32 percent (which isn’t at all bad for a four-year-old luxury compact SUV, as noted above). Further, KBB predicts a private party purchase price of $37,000, all depending on condition. The M40i’s average used-market value has genuinely moved it into new-CR-V territory, particularly if you’re comparing this top-tier model to the top-tier 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid. There is a caveat, though. Depreciation does not work on the BMW’s premium-car running costs. A luxury SUV continues to warrant luxury pricing for insurance, maintenance, repairs and parts. And there’s the added cost of premium fuel for top performance. Against the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid, the 2022 BMW X3 M40i's biggest advantage lies under the hood. Its 3.0-liter turbocharged inline-six produces 382 horsepower and 369 pound-feet of torque, and you can get an extra 11-horsepower boost from the engine’s mild hybrid system. It uses an eight-speed automatic transmission to send power to all four wheels using the standard xDrive AWD system, and includes adaptive M Suspension, variable sport steering and performance control. Acceleration to 60 mph is rated by BMW at 4.4 seconds and listed by various sources in the 4.1–4.2-second range. However, it prefers premium fuel, though regular is acceptable and premium is recommended for top performance, and its fuel economy is rated by the EPA at just 23 mpg combined, which borders on big-engine guzzling. The X3 M40i is a performance compact that happens to have five seats and useful cargo space. The side benefit of choosing the 2022 BMW X3 M40i over a 2026 Honda CR-V is the expected, and sometimes innovative, luxury-SUV treatment—powered sport front seats with lumbar adjustment and thigh extensions, panoramic sunroof, three-zone climate control, keyless entry, power tailgate, premium sound system, and a comprehensive suite of driving aids. Its interior room and versatility are compact-SUV average, with seating for five, 101.4 cubic feet of passenger volume, and 28.7 cubic feet of cargo space (expandable to 62.7). Seating is upright and airy, with about 40 inches of headroom, and 36.7 inches of rear-seat legroom. As you'll discover later, it's smaller than the 2026 CR-V, but hardly a compromised sport sedan wearing an SUV body style. Imagine time-traveling between automotive timelines, in which the current Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid is visited by a BMW X3 M40i from the past. The two were never meant to occupy the same economic universe, but the warping of the space/time continuum means the four-year-old BMW X3 is able to compete on equal footing with the present-day Honda CR-V. Pitting the speed, mechanical sophistication and luxury of the former against the latter’s efficiency, practicality and modern value creates an interesting dynamic. On paper, they look like visitors from entirely different galaxies. In the real-world battle of used versus new, however, they become worthy adversaries. Which one comes out on top? Let’s find out. The mechanical force between the 2022 BMW X3 M40i and 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid are extremes of the same energy. The X3 M40i is aggressive and emotional, wielding 382 horsepower and 369 pound-feet of torque, an eight-speed transmission and performance tuned xDrive AWD to blast to 60 mph in a claimed 4.4 seconds. The CR-V Hybrid is peaceful and aims to stay in harmony with its environment, with a 204-horsepower 2.0-liter dual-motor hybrid powertrain and continuously variable transmission delivering EPA ratings of 40 mpg/34 mpg/37 mpg (city/highway/combined). Compact SUV battles, especially those involving family values, are fought in interior comfort, space and versatility. The BMW X3 M40i is bigger in overall footprint, but only marginally—an inch in overall length and width—and rides on a six-inch longer wheelbase, giving it a more stable stance from which to attack. Theoretically, it should have the larger interior, but the Honda counterstrikes with two more cubic feet of passenger volume, six inches more overall legroom, and 9.5 cubic feet more of cargo volume (expanding to nearly 14 more cubic feet when the rear seats are folded down). That gives the CR-V Hybrid the higher ground when the mission involves passengers, luggage and the real-world realities of family life. The X3's dark-side temptation starts to overpower its emotional appeal when you factor in the costs of ownership. Depending on region and demographics, the 2022 BMW X3 M40i carries an estimated five-year cost to own of between $72,000 and $79,000, according to Edmunds, including $11,000–$12,500 in projected maintenance and insurance in the $3,000–$7,500 range, as well as EPA-estimated annual fuel costs of $3,300. In contrast, the 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid remains serene, with Edmunds' estimated costs ranging from $42,500 to $46,500, including a swing of $4,500 to $6,000 for maintenance and $2,400–$6,600 for insurance. The EPA projects annual fuel costs at $1,650, which is half that of the 2022 X3 and signifies a difference of $8,250 over five years of ownership. Long lifespans are something Honda models are known for, and the CR-V is no exception. On the other hand, it isn't something BMW models are intrinsically known for. According to iSeeCars, the BMW X3 has an average lifespan of 130,589 miles and 11.5 years, with a five percent chance of reaching at least 200,000 miles. That's enough to land it in the number-seven spot out of the 28 most reliable luxury small SUVs. The CR-V has an average lifespan of 169,369 miles and 13.8 years, with an impressive 30.3 percent chance of reaching 200,000 miles. iSeeCars also ranks it number two out of the 66 most reliable crossover SUVs, and number two out of the 19 most reliable small SUVs. Taking things higher, the publication ranks the Honda CR-V 20th on its list of the longest-lasting cars, with a 10.6 percent chance of reaching 250,000 miles — 2.2 times the average vehicle's chances; the X3 is not mentioned on this list. Still, those figures for the X3 aren't bad overall, and for a genuine luxury SUV, they're enough to build the confidence needed to make a decision come time to purchase. The takeaway is that depreciation has created a used market in which a $42,550 Honda CR-V budget can acquire a $60,000 BMW, though that vehicle has four years of real-world experience under its belt. The 2022 BMW X3 M40i makes a convincing argument against spending $42,550 on a 2026 Honda CR-V Sport Touring Hybrid, when you look at its expected sub-$40,000 purchase price. It’s especially relevant to buyers who want more oomph and to portray more prestige from their family-SUV purchase. You could argue, though, that real-world sensibilities and restraint portray a more family-friendly mindset with the CR-V Hybrid, with the latter proving to be the more rational long-term purchase, particularly for drivers who desire a more spacious and versatile interior, and rack up more miles in urban and suburban circles, rather than racing ovals. The comparison isn’t isolated, though, with other luxury SUVs offering consideration against the CR-V. For buyers who like the CR-V formula but want more luxury while keeping it in the family, the 2024 Acura RDX SH-AWD is worth consideration, especially when it's fitted with A-Spec and Advance packages. Its original MSRP was $54,150, and it’s currently fair-priced by KBB at $38,900. The platform is similar, but the differences are many—a 2.0-liter turbocharged "four," AWD, and a more premium cabin, but also an EPA-projected $3,300 fuel bill and a $54,000–$62,500 Edmunds True Cost-To-Own range. On the domestic side, the 2025 Cadillac XT4 Sport is available in the $39,400 range (according to KBB), down just over five percent from its original MSRP of $41,595, but that is the FWD model. Choosing the AWD model would drive the price beyond the 2026 CR-V ceiling, taking it to $47,500–$50,300 (according to J.D. Power). With the Cadillac, you also get a 2.0-liter turbocharged four-cylinder (rated at 225 horsepower) and a $63,000–$66,000 true cost to own over five years (around $4,500 on maintenance), but you don't spend as much on fuel as the other luxury compact SUV considerations (around $3,000 per year). Sources: BMW, Honda, iSeeCars, Edmunds, Kelley Blue Book, the EPA, J.D. Power We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. title: The People v. Gorilla Grodd Is a Great Idea at the Worst Possible Time for DC - Yahoo
content: The People v. Gorilla Grodd is a great example of an interesting idea that comes at the worst possible time for DC. The Superman universe is heading to television. HBO Max has given The People v. Gorilla Grodd a straight-to-series order. The half-hour comedy will see Skyler Gisondo reprise his role from Superman as Jimmy Olsen, the reporter who works alongside Lois Lane at the Daily Planet. Jimmy Tatro will play Gorilla Grodd, the notorious villain who gains significant mental powers after a chance encounter with an alien spacecraft. The official logline reads, "A superintelligent ape is convicted of murdering his father, the King of Gorilla City. In an eight-part true crime docuseries, the Daily Planet's Jimmy Olsen reopens the case, investigating whether Gorilla Grodd was wrongly convicted in one of Metropolis' most famous murder trials." Tony Yacenda and Dan Perrault will serve as showrunners, writers, and executive producers. The series will be presented as a true-crime mockumentary series. The People vs. Gorilla Grodd is an innovative series that could be a successful venture. It's also a major risk that the DCU should not be exploring right now. I respect DC heads James Gunn and Peter Safran for thinking outside of the box. DC is not Marvel. Therefore, it should pursue fresh and innovative ideas for its shows. Building Lanterns as a superhero version of True Detective was a smart decision. Allowing the creative duo behind American Vandal to make a DC show in a similar style is a fun proposition. I even think the show has a chance to be good. However, it's not what the DCU needs right now. Supergirl's failure was a major dent in the DCU's momentum following Superman. Questions are now being asked whether Gunn and Safran are the right minds to lead the DC forward. The early success of Lanterns is a nice rebound, but it doesn't fix DC's movie problem. Can DC stories without Batman or Superman at the center succeed? We'll find out again in October with Clayface. The People v. Gorilla Grodd is too risky a proposition right now. DC needs major hits right now to justify its plans for the DCU. It cannot have a Supergirl-like failure again. The DCU should be going all-in on Superman and Batman before expanding to niche characters from those universes. Jimmy Olsen and Gorilla Grodd are in the Superman universe, but do mainstream audiences know that? Olsen might be a maybe, but it's definitely a "no" for Gorilla Grodd. At least casual fans knew about The Penguin from The Batman. If this were a Lex Luthor show instead of a Gorilla Grodd show, that makes more sense. Gorilla Grodd could one day be worthy of a TV show. Even if it's good, right now is not the time. Originally published by Dan Girolamo at SuperHeroHype The post The People v. title: The American V8 Sedan Built For Old-School Drivers - Top Speed
content: There is something increasingly unusual about a modern performance sedan that asks its driver to do some of the work. As the industry moves toward smaller turbocharged engines, electrification, all-wheel drive, and transmissions that shift faster than any human could, one American sedan continues to make a different argument. It does not need to reinvent the formula. Instead, it doubles down on the ingredients that made high-performance cars so compelling in the first place. A big V8, rear-wheel drive, a manual transmission, and enough power to overwhelm the rear tires. The result is a sedan that feels almost rebellious in an increasingly digital performance-car world. The engine is the first clue that this Cadillac was developed with a very different philosophy from most modern performance sedans. Under the hood sits a hand-built 6.2-liter supercharged V8, rather than a smaller twin-turbocharged six-cylinder or four-cylinder. It uses a cam-in-block architecture with two valves per cylinder, direct injection, and active fuel management. On premium gasoline, it produces 668 horsepower at 6,500 rpm and 659 pound-feet of torque at 3,600 rpm. Cadillac quotes a 0-to-60 mph time of just 3.4 seconds. Those numbers are important, but the way the engine produces them matters just as much. A supercharger delivers its boost differently from a turbocharger. There is no waiting for exhaust gases to build pressure before the engine responds. The result is an immediate, muscular connection between throttle input and acceleration. Press the accelerator and the V8 answers with a surge that feels linear, forceful, and distinctly mechanical. We had the grand opportunity to test drive the CT5-V Blackwing with the Precision Package, which is its most track-oriented avatar. Our first impressions revolved around how gorgeous it was in Radiant Red, though the appearance stood second once we actually stepped on the gas pedal. We stated that "you don't drive the Blackwing so much as you hold on for dear life" — a telling sentiment for a car built around total nonsense. And when we say "nonsense," we mean it in the most flattering way possible, as our test drive was one for the ages. From the acceleration to the handling, and everything in between, it impressed us, which led us to compare it to Mercedes-AMG's Black Series and BMW M's CS models — the highest-caliber performance on the road. The "LT4" supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 is an absolute monster. It gives the rear-wheel-drive CT5-V Blackwing a furious acceleration that I honestly haven't experienced much of in any other performance car. It's a 200+ mile-per-hour car, and it definitely feels like it. Interior-wise, don't expect anything less than genuine luxury. The seats are a standout feature — supportive, but not overly firm; elegant, but not overly styled. It's essentially a Goldilocks car that we're not likely to see ever again. The best part is that it's an actual sedan, not just in door count, but in size. There's plenty of room for passengers, and the trunk offers enough cargo space for luggage and groceries. On top of all that, it's well-insulated from outside noise, with the only sound trickling through being the glorious V8 roar. The way it should be. The engine would already make the Blackwing special, but Cadillac went considerably further. Power is sent exclusively to the rear wheels, and the standard transmission is a six-speed manual. A 10-speed automatic is available, but the manual is the combination that best captures the philosophy behind this car. That matters because 668 horsepower is not a number that can simply be switched off by an electronic safety net. The driver has to manage it. The six-speed manual puts the driver directly into the process. Selecting the correct gear, judging engine speed, modulating the clutch and controlling throttle application become part of the experience. With 659 pound-feet available, there is always enough torque to punish a sloppy input, but that is also part of the appeal. Modern performance cars increasingly do an enormous amount of the thinking for their drivers. All-wheel-drive systems distribute torque between axles, dual-clutch transmissions execute near-instantaneous shifts and sophisticated stability systems intervene before mistakes become expensive. The Blackwing certainly has sophisticated electronics of its own. It features Performance Traction Management, an electronic limited-slip differential, launch control, Magnetic Ride Control, and selectable drive modes. Its Brembo brakes are designed to handle repeated hard use, while an available carbon-ceramic setup provides even greater stopping power. But those systems support the driver rather than replacing the experience. The rear-drive layout is particularly important. Instead of simply launching with all four tires clawing for traction, the Blackwing makes its rear axle an active participant in the driving experience. Throttle application can alter the car's attitude, and the driver can exploit the enormous grip available from its wide performance tires. The result is a sedan that can be driven quickly without feeling clinical. It feels like a machine. Turbocharging has become the dominant solution for extracting more performance from smaller engines while improving efficiency and emissions. The regular CT5-V, for example, uses a 3.0-liter twin-turbocharged V6 producing 360 horsepower and 405 pound-feet. The Blackwing takes a completely different route, using twice the cylinders and more than twice the displacement per cylinder to deliver its performance. It is not the most efficient way to build a fast sedan. Cadillac itself rates the Blackwing at just 13 mpg city and 20 mpg highway. But efficiency was clearly not the primary objective here. The objective was character. The engine also gives the Blackwing an unmistakable soundtrack. The supercharged V8's induction noise, mechanical whine, and exhaust note combine to create an experience that simply cannot be replicated by a smaller turbocharged engine or an electric motor. That makes the Blackwing unusual before it even moves. This is where the Blackwing stops being merely an interesting alternative and becomes something genuinely extraordinary. Cadillac gives the sedan 668 horsepower, 659 pound-feet of torque and a manufacturer-estimated 3.4-second sprint to 60 mph. It can exceed 200 mph on a racetrack, according to Cadillac. Those figures put the Blackwing firmly into super-sedan territory. Yet the most impressive part is not simply that it is fast. Plenty of modern sedans are brutally quick. The difference is that the Blackwing combines that speed with a package that remains unusually focused on driver involvement. Magnetic Ride Control continuously adapts the suspension, while the performance-oriented chassis, electronic limited-slip differential and Performance Traction Management system allow the car to transition between road-going comfort and serious track capability. The brakes are equally serious. Brembo hardware is fitted at both ends, with slotted performance rotors standard and carbon-ceramic brakes available for buyers who intend to spend significant time on a circuit. The car also rides on 19-inch forged wheels with high-performance tires, including 275-section rubber at the front and 305-section tires at the rear. That combination gives the Blackwing the hardware to exploit its engine rather than merely advertise it. And yet it remains a genuine sedan. There are five seats, 11.9 cubic feet of cargo space and a cabin designed to function as a luxury interior rather than a stripped-out race-car cockpit. Cadillac quotes 42.4 inches of front legroom and 37 inches of rear legroom. That dual personality is one of the Blackwing's greatest strengths. It can be a brutally fast driver's car on Saturday morning and still function as a reasonably practical luxury sedan during the week. For 2026, Cadillac lists the CT5-V Blackwing at $98,900 before options, putting it firmly into expensive territory but also making its mechanical specification remarkable for the money. Calling the Blackwing "old school" does not mean calling it primitive. Inside, the car is packed with technology. Cadillac offers heated and massaging front seats, a heated steering wheel, premium materials, carbon-fiber trim, and a 33-inch display with Google built-in. An AKG 16-speaker audio system is also available, while Super Cruise can provide hands-free driving assistance on compatible roads. That combination is important because the Blackwing does not reject modern luxury. It simply refuses to let technology become the entire personality of the car. The suspension can absorb ordinary road imperfections. The seats can provide the sort of comfort expected from a modern Cadillac. The technology can handle navigation, entertainment, and driver assistance. Then the driver presses the V button, selects a gear, and finds an entirely different machine underneath. That contrast is what makes the Blackwing so compelling. There is also something reassuringly physical about the controls. A manual shifter moves through a defined gate. A clutch pedal has to be operated. The engine responds to throttle position. The rear axle responds to power. The driver can feel the consequences of their decisions. That is increasingly unusual. Even some of the world's most accomplished performance sedans have moved toward turbocharged engines, automatic transmissions and all-wheel drive. Those cars are extraordinarily capable, often faster in the real world and easier to drive quickly. But they can also create a layer of separation between the person behind the wheel and the machine underneath. Calling any car the "last" of anything is risky. Automotive history rarely follows a perfectly predictable path. But the evidence makes the Blackwing's position increasingly difficult to ignore. The formula it represents is disappearing. A large-displacement supercharged V8 is already an increasingly unusual choice in a new performance sedan. A rear-wheel-drive layout is becoming less common as manufacturers pursue all-weather traction and increasingly sophisticated torque-vectoring systems. And a six-speed manual transmission has become almost exotic in the luxury performance segment. The Blackwing combines all three. More importantly, Cadillac is not merely keeping the configuration alive as a symbolic gesture. It continues to offer the 668-horsepower supercharged V8 with the six-speed manual for the 2026 model year. Cadillac lists the car as having extremely limited availability, while a special Curated by Cadillac version is being hand-built in Michigan with production beginning in mid-2026. That special model's approximately $158,000 starting price also demonstrates just how exclusive the formula can become. The company now sells electric performance models alongside combustion-powered V-Series cars, including the 519-horsepower Optiq-V and the electric Lyriq-V. The CT4-V Blackwing uses a twin-turbocharged V6 rather than a V8, while the CT5-V Blackwing remains the flagship expression of Cadillac's traditional high-output formula. That broader industry shift makes the Blackwing more significant. The argument is not that electric or turbocharged performance cars are worse. In many measurable respects, they are faster, more efficient and more technologically advanced. The argument is that the Blackwing represents a type of car that is becoming harder to build under modern efficiency, emissions, and electrification pressures. A 6.2-liter supercharged V8 powering the rear wheels through a manual transmission is almost an act of defiance. And that is why the Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing matters to enthusiasts. It is a reminder that performance is not defined solely by acceleration numbers. It is also about noise, vibration, shifting, throttle control, and the small decisions that allow a driver to feel responsible for what the car does next. We want to hear from you. Outside the exhibition hangers at Sun 'n Fun, Viking Aircraft Engines had its usual location and as I walked up, I was greeted by, well, a pair of Vikings, and that wasn't even the most unusual thing I saw at their tent. What was more unusual was the backdrop: a twin-engine aircraft! If you are not familiar with Viking Aircraft Engines, Jan Eggenfellner and his team have been modifying automotive engines for flight use for over 30 years and have over ten years of specializing in converting Honda's K20 series engine. Of late, quite a few of these engines have found their way on to the front of Zenith aircraft, notably the CH750. After years of developing engines and firewall forward kits for other airframe makers, Viking is now preparing to offer its own aircraft kit, a high wing twin called the V-42. The V-42 nomenclature stands for four people, two engines, or as the Eggenfellners noted in their case, "two people and four wiener dogs." Why a twin for a first kit offering? Because, according to Jan, he wanted some differentiation amongst a field of single engine kits, saying, "I think there is a market for a light, EAB easy-to-build twin. The overall goal is to provide a twin that people can afford to build and fly." The V-42's roomy forward cabin and fixed gear. [Credit: Andrew Robinson] The all-aluminum structure shows the pre-punched, pull-riveted construction. [Credit: Andrew Robinson] At first, "easy-to-build" and "affordable" sound like aviation oxymorons but based on what I saw at the show it certainly looks feasible. The entire aircraft has been designed and virtually assembled in the computer, the parts formed with pre-punched holes and assembled with pull rivets. The principal difference between assembling this kit and those of others offering pre-punched holes is simply one of size and having enough space to do it. If you are wondering about space, the one-piece wing is just over 38 feet long with a chord of roughly five feet. Did I mention one-piece? This isn't a wing to build in the spare bedroom, and probably not in the garage, either. My garage measures only 30 feet deep. Plan accordingly. Also, the rivets are big; if you don't have a pneumatic rivet puller, get one or go ahead and schedule your carpal tunnel surgery now. I observed that the wing does not have flaps and was told that by removing the flaps and associated structure, the wing is lighter and stronger, plus has more area for carrying more load, resulting in lower wing loading overall. The lower wing loading, combined with counter-rotating engines, fixed gear, and the absence of flaps are all intended to make this a fairly easy aircraft to fly, "Like a twin-engine Cub," noted Jan. If you're like me, you want to know the numbers, so here are some of the more pertinent ones: How does a twin hav a combined ten-gallon per hour fuel burn? By using Honda K-series based engines that run in the Otto cycle for takeoff power, and Atkinson cycle mode for higher efficiency during the cruise phase of flight. These will be higher horse-power engines derated to 150 hp. For other numbers, I was told to figure approximately $75,000 for the chassis on its gear, and around $150,000 for a "bare bones" completed aircraft, going up from there depending on choices of avionics, paint, and interior. The goal is to have the prototype flying sometime this summer, and from there begin refining one area of the aircraftat a time prior to releasing kits. From behind, the V-42's tall tail and long, flap-less high wing are clear. [Credit: Andrew Robinson] For an aircraft of this size, one might assume that this would be one of those with the mandatory builder assist, but the V-42 can be offered as an EAB kit, and my guess is that it probably will.  (That will make for some serious boxes in the driveway). Whether or not there will be a builder assist program is to be determined, in response to that question. At this time, January 2027 is the target date for the first kit to be available, with Eggenfellner saying it will likely be the rudder. We'll be keeping an eye on development and will be looking to have a flight review of what could indeed be an every-person's twin available in a later issue. title: Canada-Built Toyota RAV4, Honda CR-V Miss Out on Tariff Relief - Autoguide.com
content: A draft agreement that would have cut U.S. duties on Canadian-made vehicles to 15% collapsed at the last minute. That leaves models such as the Toyota RAV4 Hybrid, Honda CR-V, and Chevrolet Silverado exposed to higher import costs. New 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods have since taken effect, according to Bloomberg, with Prime Minister Mark Carney preparing to retaliate. The failed deal would have gone beyond vehicles. Negotiators had discussed lowering tariffs on some Canadian steel and aluminum to 25%, cutting vehicle duties to 15%, and eliminating the 10% lumber tariff. Instead, talks broke down. Both sides have blamed each other. The U.S. said last-minute demands from Canadian negotiators derailed a draft that had taken days to assemble, ending the process when Canada sought additional concessions it did not specify. Canada countered that the U.S. shifted its position, saying "Last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal." Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window. For automakers, the collapse matters most on the cost side rather than at the window sticker. Lower duties on Canadian-built vehicles exported to the U.S. would have reduced expenses for dealers and manufacturers. Those savings would not necessarily have translated into lower prices, but they could have eased pressure for increases and helped preserve cross-border production and sales. With the deal dead, that relief is off the table. The new U.S. tariffs took effect Aug. 22. They cover a range of Canadian imports including plywood, liquor, electrical equipment, and hockey gear. Carney has promised dollar-for-dollar retaliation, along with additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses. The U.S. has not detailed how it would respond to that retaliation. The broader trade relationship has been under strain since the Trump administration imposed higher import tariffs, and the fallout has already reshaped some automaker plans. Unifor says Stellantis is now considering selling its Brampton Assembly Plant in Ontario. The factory was originally slated to build the next-generation Jeep Compass. But U.S. tariffs complicated the business case, and production shifted to Illinois. Vehicles are only one front in the dispute. The U.S. has also criticized Canada for allowing up to 49,000 Chinese-made EVs annually at a reduced 6.1% tariff. That arrangement could give automakers such as BYD and Geely a stronger foothold near the U.S. market, while allowing Tesla to sell lower-priced Shanghai-built models in Canada. For Toyota and Honda, the outcome leaves two of their highest-volume North American products built on the wrong side of a hardening border. The RAV4 Hybrid and CR-V remain subject to the full duty structure rather than the 15% rate that briefly appeared within reach. title: There is no constitutional “right to privacy” - SCOTUSblog
content: This is the second of five introductory articles on the relevance for U.S. constitutional law of the “born free and equal” clauses, which appeared in the Declaration of Independence and six out of 12 state constitutions when the federal Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791. The Massachusetts Constitution of 1780, for example, provided that: In my inaugural column, I showed that the born-free-and-equal idea is also reflected in, among other places: 1) Justice Bushrod Washington’s seminal 1823 opinion in Corfield v. Coryell; 2) 1848’s Seneca Falls Declaration of Sentiments, adapting the language of the Declaration of Independence in defense of sex equality; 3) President Abraham Lincoln’s Gettysburg Address; 4) the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights; and 5) Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.’s “I have a Dream” speech. I want in this second column to argue that the born-free-and-equal idea, unlike ideas such as the “right to privacy,” so permeates the Constitution that it is “deeply rooted in American history and tradition” as that phrase is used in such landmark, correctly-decided, cases as Washington v. Glucksberg (rejecting a right to assisted suicide), McDonald v. City of Chicago (recognizing that the Second Amendment’s right to own a handgun for self-protection extends to the states), Timbs v. Indiana (recognizing that the Eighth Amendment’s excessive fines clause applies to the states), and Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (rejecting the constitutional right to an abortion). Unlike the so-called right to privacy, the born free and equal clauses were specifically enumerated in the bills of rights of 24 out of 37 states when the 14th Amendment was ratified in 1868, and this right was enumerated in 37 out of 50 state bills of rights when I last checked in 2018. At the same time, the born free and equal clauses, constitutionalized by the 14th Amendment in 1868, are subject to an important caveat. As Senator Jacob Howard, in his Report to the U.S. Senate on Behalf of the Joint Committee on Reconstruction delivered on May 23, 1866, explicitly stated: The language above in bold face is Justice Washington’s paraphrase of the born free and equal clauses. But, as noted, the language above in italics imposes a very important limit on the individual rights that courts can find. It is the language in italics that gives us the rational basis test whereby “just” laws, enacted “for the general good of the whole [people]” must nevertheless be upheld if they survive what I would call rational basis review “with bite.” This all contrasts markedly with the supposed right to privacy recognized in some of the court’s landmark cases. A substantial majority of the American people in 1791, 1868, and 2018 lived in states which had born free and equal clauses, but almost no Americans in 1791, 1868, or 2018 lived in states whose bills of rights guarantee a right to privacy. Let us take the 1965 case of Griswold v. Connecticut, in which the supposed right to privacy was partially established. In Griswold, the court considered the constitutionality of a state law which banned the use of contraceptives by married couples. Writing for the majority, Justice William O. Douglas determined that this violated a right to privacy found in “penumbras, formed by emanations from [the Bill of Right’s] guarantees that help give them life and substance.” I disagree: 1) with Douglas’ opinion with its embarrassing reference to a right to privacy with no historical antecedents and to the so-called “emanations and penumbras” of the Bill of Rights; 2) with Justice Arthur Goldberg’s embarrassing position that such a right can be found in the Ninth Amendment instead, which is totally ahistorical as to how it applies to the 14th Amendment; and 3) with Justice John Marshall Harlan’s evolving common law substantive due process opinion. The opinion in Griswold which comes the closest to being correct is Justice Byron White’s concurrence, which stresses the lack of means-end fit between a highly intrusive ban on the use of contraceptives by married couples and its goal to discourage adultery. The ban by Connecticut on the use of contraceptives by married couples was not unconstitutional because it violated a right to privacy, but on the basis that it was a law which the government may not “justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” This was because: 1) Connecticut was the only state out of 50 with a ban on the use of contraceptives by married couples, making it an extreme outlying jurisdiction; 2) Connecticut’s law criminalizing contraceptive use by married couples was never enforced, and the plaintiff himself had to go to great lengths even to get prosecuted; 3) the rationale advanced to defend the Connecticut law that it discourages adultery was absurd on its face (for the reasons given in White’s concurrence); 4) married couples cannot “enjoy and defend liberty” or “seek and obtain safety and happiness” if their access to birth control is denied for the state’s preposterous reason that doing so might somehow inhibit adultery; and 5) the Connecticut law was passed a long time ago and was not a recent attempt by a single state to experiment with a reform that it hoped would catch on in other states. Given this, it would be a great advance in constitutional law were the Supreme Court to revisit its holding in Griswold v. Connecticut and make it clear that that case was rightly decided under the privileges or immunities clause of the 14th Amendment and not under the absurd doctrine of substantive due process or under the Ninth Amendment. To take a more recent case, Chief Justice William H. Rehnquist was correct in holding that there is no unenumerated right to assisted suicide as was claimed by the plaintiff in Washington v. Glucksberg. There was an overwhelming consensus in 1791 and 1868 that laws banning assisted suicide were desirable for a whole host of reasons. Along those lines, Justice Samuel Alito in Dobbs was correct in holding that there was an overwhelming consensus in 1791 and 1868 that laws prohibiting abortion were “just[] … laws prescribed for the general good of the whole [people].” At the same time, I do not think that the born free and equal clauses mean that Lochner v. New York or Roe v. Wade were incorrectly decided simply because liberty in the abstract was implicated in those cases. Laws setting maximum working hours (as in Lochner) or restricting abortion (unlike the contraceptives law at issue in Griswold) are “restraints [which] the government may justly prescribe for the general good of the whole [people].” Such laws thus easily pass a rational basis with bite test. With respect to abortion or assisted suicide, I think that the question of when life begins, and ends, is inherently a political question. It is a question which people of different religious or secular backgrounds can and will resolve differently. The life-tenured Article III federal courts simply have no business second-guessing legislative decisions on such political issues. Federalizing and constitutionalizing the rule on these political questions is a gross abuse of power by the Supreme Court, bound to convulse the body politic (which, indeed, is what we saw in the case of Roe v. Wade). To put it differently, cases like Lochner and Roe raise what former Judge Robert H. Bork called the counter-majoritarian difficulty in a way that a case like Griswold v. Connecticut simply does not. The law Griswold struck down was barely related at all to the burdens which Connecticut’s defunct, old statute imposed. Griswold v. Connecticut is thus an exceptional and rare case in which the born free and equal clauses were violated, but not because of any constitutional right to privacy. Lochner and Roe were wrongly decided for that reason. In my next article, I will apply the born free and equal clauses with regard to whether there is a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law. title: Health of Norwegian King Harald V worsens following hospitalization - Plataforma Media
content:
The health condition of Norway’s 89-year-old monarch, King Harald V, deteriorated over the weekend as he remains hospitalized for ongoing medical complications, according to an official statement released by the Royal Palace. Europe’s oldest reigning monarch is currently undergoing treatment for hemolytic anemia, a disorder characterized by the rapid destruction of red blood cells that frequently causes severe fatigue, paleness, and respiratory difficulty. Medical staff at Oslo University Hospital are also administering antibiotics to treat a bacterial blood infection, with palace officials confirming that the king has responded to the medication. He was initially admitted early last week to manage fluid retention resulting from cortisone treatment. Following an official two-week medical leave announcement, the palace confirmed that King Harald’s scheduled visit to the central region of Trøndelag in early September has been canceled. Members of the royal family, including Queen Sonja, Crown Prince Haakon—who is currently serving as regent—Crown Princess Mette-Marit, and the king’s sister, have visited him at the hospital, though none issued public statements upon leaving. King Harald, who ascended the throne in 1991, has faced several health setbacks in recent years, including receiving a pacemaker and scaling back his public duties. Despite recurring hospitalizations, including a stay in Tenerife earlier this year for an infection and dehydration, he has consistently maintained that he will not abdicate, citing his lifelong oath to the Norwegian Parliament. The king’s health decline occurs during a challenging period for the Norwegian monarchy, marked by legal and public scrutiny involving other members of the royal family. Despite these ongoing issues, King Harald remains a largely popular and unifying figure among the Norwegian public.
